Ramtin on how investors justify paying billion-dollar entry prices

"Every few years in Silicon Valley, the goalpost moves for what terminal outcomes can be. 

When I got started in early-stage investing in 2016, people looked at every company through the lens of, 'In a best-case scenario, this could be a $10 billion outcome,' and priced deals accordingly. 

Then you got towards 2021, and everybody started looking at companies through the lens of, 'In a best-case scenario, this company can be worth $100 billion.'

And now we're at a new goalpost of, 'In a best-case scenario, this company could have a trillion-dollar outcome.' 

My bet is there might be two to three more, and not 40 more. 

But now everyone's looking at companies through the lens of, 'In a best-case scenario, you have a trillion-dollar outcome, so what is a $1 billion entry valuation in a trillion-dollar outcome scenario?'"

Yesterday the S&P 500 fell 4.36%, its worst day since 2011 outside of Covid and the April 2025 tariff shock. 

Options positioning sheds light on what exactly made this such a sharp drop: entering Thursday, dealers held negative gamma to the downside. This meant they hedged their positions by selling as prices fell, and every leg lower forced more selling.

As it stands, much of that negative gamma remains tied to the Nov 20 options expiration, so big swings in either direction remain a risk.

Several major catalysts arrive between now and then. CPI (Nov 10) and PPI (Nov 13) are the next tests, and traders are already paying up for protection through both dates.

BREAKING: Global crude oil in transit is up to 1.28 billion barrels, an all-time high.

This figure has surged +180 million barrels over the last several weeks.

This comes as Middle Eastern oil flows recover through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, while more crude remains at sea for longer.

Ship-to-ship transfers are keeping oil aboard tankers for longer, while extended shipping routes are increasing transit times.

Meanwhile, global oil importers diversifying away from the Middle East are lengthening voyages, leaving more crude tied up aboard tankers.

As a result, more oil remains in transit rather than being readily available to refiners, tightening near-term supply despite recovering export flows.

Oil is flowing, but timely delivery is becoming the bottleneck.

John: "I'm an optimist. I could not do my job if I wasn't an optimist. But just know that I see the thousands of companies every year that don't make it. Because they all come to us to try to be acquired."

“If the *legal* system can't stop millions of foreigners from *illegally* entering the country, then the legal system is some combination of biased and impotent.”

To clarify again, the legal system does not allocate resources toward problems. In this context of holding back executive overreach, what the legal system does is rule whether executive or legislative actions are legal. Border security is an executive and legislative branch function.

“Every week there’s a story of a criminal with a long rap sheet being released and committing yet another crime.”

Sure, but at this level of conversation we focus on math rather than anecdotes, right? Crime is trending *down* over decades, despite the talking points we often hear. As a result, voters don’t typically put crime in their top slot for what they vote on even though it trends here on right-of-center social media that we're both swimming in. In areas where it’s a growing problem, I’m right there with you that it should be fixed. That’s mostly a function of putting politicians into power that will write laws that give harsher sentences to repeat offenders.

“The legal system and the agencies aren’t even trying to find the fraud.”

The Justice Department is currently run by Republicans. They could put more resources there. All the DOGE public focus on fraud amounted to little. Fraud should be prosecuted of course, but it often gets over-emphasized in political discourse because it’s the easy button. It’s politicians’ way of saying they don’t want to cut benefits or raise taxes (unpopular), and instead they claim there’s this massive room to cut down on fraud (good soundbite, everyone’s against fraud, let’s fix the budget that way). And then when they’re in power, fraud is peanuts as a percentage.

“The only reason anyone would be against voter ID is because they want to cheat.”

Then the legislative branch should have passed voter ID. Part of the issue is they overreached. They wanted super strict rules that would have made it so that even most driver’s licenses wouldn’t qualify as a voting ID. Additionally, they wanted it to apply right away to these 2026 elections, and the various federal and state document offices (Passports, Birth Certificates, etc) are not fit to handle a sharp influx of document changes that would be needed in those few months (women updating their last name on birth certificates which they never bothered to do before, now that their driver’s license isn’t even sufficient to vote, etc). I know you are not naïve, so you get the background debate there. Those in favor of voter ID also find it politically favorable to add frictions to voting (fewer younger, poorer voters), and they pushed hard here, for this election. Those against voter ID also find it politically favorable to reduce frictions to voting (more younger, poorer voters). In this latest move, voter ID proponents tried too hard to be as strict as possible and couldn’t get it done because there were actually serious issues with their proposal that get glossed over by partisans. Strategic error on their part. Pushing for a driver’s license to vote or phasing things in over years could have brought in wider support and would have a had a higher chance, compared to what they tried. And again, all of this is a legislative issue, not a judicial one.

Regarding border security and partisanship, Biden had a higher rate of annual border apprehensions than any modern president. A big issue was that there were far more people trying to cross the border, given the Covid backdrop. I think border security should have been an even bigger issue, but it’s important to understand that baseline context. And then when there was a bipartisan bill in 2024 to put more resources on the border, it was Republicans who blocked it because they wanted it to be a live issue for the 2024 elections (which, from a strict strategy perspective, probably worked out).

To clarify again, the legal system does not allocate resources toward problems. In this context of holding back executive overreach, what the legal system does is rule whether executive or legislative actions are legal. Border security is an executive and legislative branch function.

“Every week there’s a story of a criminal with a long rap sheet being released and committing yet another crime.”

Sure, but at this level of conversation we focus on math rather than anecdotes, right? Crime is trending *down* over decades, despite the talking points we often hear. As a result, voters don’t typically put crime in their top slot for what they vote on even though it trends here on right-of-center social media that we're both swimming in. In areas where it’s a growing problem, I’m right there with you that it should be fixed. That’s mostly a function of putting politicians into power that will write laws that give harsher sentences to repeat offenders.

“The legal system and the agencies aren’t even trying to find the fraud.”

The Justice Department is currently run by Republicans. They could put more resources there. All the DOGE public focus on fraud amounted to little. Fraud should be prosecuted of course, but it often gets over-emphasized in political discourse because it’s the easy button. It’s politicians’ way of saying they don’t want to cut benefits or raise taxes (unpopular), and instead they claim there’s this massive room to cut down on fraud (good soundbite, everyone’s against fraud, let’s fix the budget that way). And then when they’re in power, fraud is peanuts as a percentage.

“The only reason anyone would be against voter ID is because they want to cheat.”

Then the legislative branch should have passed voter ID. Part of the issue is they overreached. They wanted super strict rules that would have made it so that even most driver’s licenses wouldn’t qualify as a voting ID. Additionally, they wanted it to apply right away to these 2026 elections, and the various federal and state document offices (Passports, Birth Certificates, etc) are not fit to handle a sharp influx of document changes that would be needed in those few months (women updating their last name on birth certificates which they never bothered to do before, now that their driver’s license isn’t even sufficient to vote, etc). I know you are not naïve, so you get the background debate there. Those in favor of voter ID also find it politically favorable to add frictions to voting (fewer younger, poorer voters), and they pushed hard here, for this election. Those against voter ID also find it politically favorable to reduce frictions to voting (more younger, poorer voters). In this latest move, voter ID proponents tried too hard to be as strict as possible and couldn’t get it done because there were actually serious issues with their proposal that get glossed over by partisans. And again, all of this is a legislative issue, not a judicial one.

A big issue was that there were far more people trying to cross the border, given the Covid backdrop. I think border security should have been an even bigger issue, but it’s important to understand that baseline context.
